mekki-muskil:2-2.t:
His saying, exalted is He, {أَن يتْركُوا}: أن is in the position of the accusative by حسب.
His saying {أَن يَقُولُوا}: أن is in the position of the accusative by omission of the preposition, i.e. "with (بأن) their saying" or "because (لأن) they say". It is also said that it is a badal (substitute) for the first.

mekki-muskil:4-4.t: His saying {سَاءَ مَا يحكمون}: ما is in the position of the accusative and it is indefinite, i.e. "evil is a thing that they judge". It is also said that ما is in the position of the nominative and it is definite, its implied form being "evil is the thing that they judge". Ibn Kaysān said: ما with the verb is a maṣdar (verbal noun) in the position of the nominative, its implied form being "evil is their judgement".

mekki-muskil:8-8.t: His saying {بِوَالِديهِ حسنا}: i.e. "We enjoined him concerning his parents (a matter) possessing goodness" (ذَا حسن). Then He put the adjective in place of the described noun, which is الأمر ("the matter"); then the muḍāf, which is ذا, was omitted, and the muḍāf ilayhi, which is حسن, was put in its place.

mekki-muskil:12-12.t:
His saying {ولنحمل خطاياكم}: its wording is imperative and its meaning is condition and recompense (al-sharṭ wa-l-jazāʾ). ٢
[Translator's note: the numeral ٢ at the end appears in the source text as written; it seems to be a stray marker.]

mekki-muskil:14-14.t:
His saying {ألف سنة}: ألف is accusative as an adverb of time, and خمسين is accusative by exception. According to Sībawayh the excepted noun is accusative only because it is like the object, since it is dispensable like the object, and it came after the sentence was complete, so it was made accusative like the object. Its accusative according to al-Farrāʾ is by أنّ; in his view the origin (of إلا) is إنّ لا: when it puts in the accusative it does so by أنّ, and when it puts in the nominative it does so by لا. Its accusative according to al-Mubarrad is as a mafʿūl bihi (direct object); in his view إلا stands in place of the verb that puts the noun in the accusative, so it stands in place of "I except so-and-so". According to most grammarians, from a number only less than half may be excepted.
{وَلَقَد أرسلنَا نوحًا}: i.e. "and We sent Abraham". It is also said that it is accusative by an implied verb, i.e. "and remember Abraham".
[Translator's note: the explanation "We sent Abraham" belongs to {وَإِبْرَاهِيم} (29:16); the source attaches it here to the quotation {وَلَقَد أرسلنَا نوحًا} as written.]

mekki-muskil:16-16.t:
His saying {وَإِبْرَاهِيم إِذْ قَالَ}: إبراهيم is accusative by conjunction to the hāʾ in فأنجيناه. It is also said that it is conjoined to نوح in His saying
[Translator's note: the source sentence breaks off here; presumably the intended reference is {وَلَقَد أرسلنَا نوحًا} (29:14).]

mekki-muskil:22-22.t: His saying {وَمَا أَنْتُم بمعجزين فِي الأَرْض وَلَا فِي السَّمَاء}: i.e. "nor is whoever is in the heaven able to escape", so في السماء is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted من, in the position of the nominative, and then the adjective stands in place of the noun it describes. There is something far-fetched in this, because the adjective of an indefinite noun is like the ṣila (relative clause) for it, and it is not good to omit the relative noun and have the ṣila stand in its place, though omission in the case of the adjective is better than in the case of the ṣila.

mekki-muskil:25-25.t:
His saying وَقَالَ إِنَّمَا اخذتم من دون الله أوثانا مَوَدَّة بَيْنكُم: ما has the meaning of الذي and it is the ism (noun) of إنّ, and the hāʾ (returning to ما) is implied, its implied form being "those whom you took…" (إن الذين اتخذتموهم). أوثانا is the second object of اتخذتم, and the omitted hāʾ is the first object of اتخذتم. مودة is the khabar (predicate) of إنّ. It is also said that it is nominative by an implied "it is" (هي مودة). It is also said that it is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject) and في الحياة الدنيا is the khabar, and the clause is the khabar of إنّ. بينكم is genitive because مودة is annexed to it. It is permissible to make what they took besides Allah "affection" by extension (ittisāʿ); the correct analysis of that is for the implied form to be "those whom you took as idols besides Allah are possessors of affection among you".
It has been read with مودة in the accusative, on the basis that ما is a restraining particle (kāffa) preventing إنّ from governing, so there is no omitted pronoun in اتخذتم, and أوثانا is the object of اتخذتم, since it takes one object and is restricted to it, as He said {إِن الَّذين اتَّخذُوا الْعجل سينالهم}; and مودة is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), i.e. "you only took idols besides Allah for the sake of the affection among you, not because the idols have any benefit or harm".
Whoever gives tanwīn to مودة, whether in the accusative or the nominative, makes بينكم an adverb and puts it in the accusative — that is the original, and the annexation is an extension in speech — and the governor of the adverb is المودة. In the reading of whoever gives tanwīn to مودة, you may also put بينكم in the accusative as an adjective of the maṣdar (verbal noun), because it is indefinite, and indefinite nouns are described by adverbs, clauses and verbs. If you put بينكم in the accusative as an adverb, His saying {فِي الْحَيَاة الدُّنْيَا} may also be an adverb for المودة; both are attached to the governor, which is مودة, because they are two adverbs of place or two adverbs of time, and there is no pronoun in either of these two adverbs, since neither of them stands in place of an implied omitted word.
If you make His saying بينكم an adjective of مودة, it is attached to an omitted word and contains a pronoun that was in the omitted word, which is the adjective in reality. Then في الحياة الدنيا is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from that pronoun in بينكم; its governor is the adverb, which is بينكم, and in the adverb في الحياة الدنيا there is a pronoun returning to the one in that state (dhū al-ḥāl). An adjective must contain a returning pronoun referring to the noun described; so when an adverb stands in place of the adjective, that pronoun comes to be in the adverb, just as it is in the adverb when it is the khabar of a mubtadaʾ or a ḥāl — its explanation has already been given. In this case, مودة may not govern His saying في الحياة الدنيا, which is a ḥāl from the pronoun in بينكم, because you have already described the maṣdar with His saying بينكم, and (the maṣdar) does not govern after the adjective, since what it governs is inside its ṣila (relative complement) whereas the adjective is not inside the ṣila, so you would have separated the ṣila from what it belongs to. So when it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in بينكم, only بينكم governs it, and it contains a pronoun returning to the pronoun in بينكم, being the same thing, because every ḥāl must contain a pronoun returning to the one in that state, like the adjective. Further, if you make His saying في الحياة الدنيا a ḥāl from the pronoun in بينكم, and the pronoun in بينكم is nominative only by the adverb, then the governor of the ḥāl must also be the adverb, because the governor of the one in the state is always the governor of the ḥāl, since the ḥāl is the same thing in meaning. So the governor of the two does not differ; for if it differed, two governors would have governed one thing, since the ḥāl is the possessor of the ḥāl, and so the governor of the two does not differ.
في الحياة الدنيا may also be an adjective of مودة, with بينكم also an adjective. Then each of them must contain a pronoun returning to المودة, and their governor is the omitted word which is the adjective in reality and in which the pronoun was; when the adverb stood in its place, the pronoun moved to the adverb, just as it moves to adverbs when they are predicates of a mubtadaʾ. The implied form of the omitted words is as though He said "you have only taken idols besides Allah, an affection settled among you, established in the life of this world". Then "settled" (مستقرة), containing a pronoun, and "established" (ثابتة), containing a pronoun — both returning to المودة — were omitted, and بينكم stood in place of مستقرة, which is the adjective, so the pronoun that was in it, referring to the described noun, came to be in بينكم, and it became an adjective of المودة because it is a substitute for the adjective. Likewise ثابتة, containing a pronoun, was omitted and you put في الحياة الدنيا in its place, so the pronoun came to be in your saying في الحياة الدنيا. So that omitted word is the governor of the two adverbs, and they stood in place of the two omitted adjectives and became two adjectives containing two pronouns returning to the described noun. Everything similar to this is judged by analogy with it. So understand this question, for in it I have uncovered for you the hidden secrets and rare points of grammar.

mekki-muskil:27-27.t: His saying {وَإنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَة لمن الصَّالِحين}: the preposition in His saying في الآخرة is attached to an omitted word, its implied form being "and indeed he, righteous in the Hereafter, is among the righteous". It is also said that it is a clarification (tabyīn) placed first. It is also said that it is attached to الصالحين, and the alif and lām are for definiteness and do not have the meaning of الذين.

mekki-muskil:28-28.t:
His saying {ولوطا إِذْ قَالَ لِقَوْمِهِ}: it is conjoined to the hāʾ in أنجيناه. It is also said that it is conjoined back to Noah, peace be upon him, in His saying, exalted is He, {وَلَقَد أرسلنَا نوحًا}. It is also said that it is accusative on the implied form "and remember Lot", and the governor of إذ is the governor of لوط.
[Translator's note: the text says اذا, while the verse has إِذْ.]

mekki-muskil:38-38.t: His saying {وعادا وَثَمُود}: conjoined to الذين in His saying, exalted is He, {وَلَقَد فتنا الَّذين من قبلهم}, (i.e.) "and ʿĀd and Thamūd". It is also said that it is conjoined to the hāʾ and mīm in His saying {فَأَخَذتهم الرجفة}, which is closer than the first. It is also said that the implied form is "and We destroyed ʿĀd and Thamūd".

mekki-muskil:39-39.t: His saying {وَقَارُون وَفرْعَوْن وهامان}: conjoined to عاد in all its aspects. They are foreign, definite names, and therefore they are not fully inflected (diptotes). It is also said that they are conjoined to the hāʾ and mīm in His saying, exalted is He, {فصدهم عَن السَّبِيل}, i.e. "and he hindered Qārūn, Pharaoh and Hāmān".

mekki-muskil:41-41.t: His saying {كَمثل العنكبوت}: the kāf is in the position of the nominative as the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ (subject), which is His saying, exalted is He, {مثل الَّذين اتَّخذُوا}. It is also said that it is in the position of the accusative as an adverb. The plural of العنكبوت is عناكيب, عناكب, عكاب, عكب and أعكب.

mekki-muskil:46-46.t: His saying {إِلَّا الَّذين ظلمُوا}: الذين is in the position of the accusative as a badal (substitute) for أهل, or by exception.

mekki-muskil:51-51.t: His saying {أَو لم يَكفهمْ أَنا أنزلنَا}: أن is in the position of the nominative as the fāʿil (agent) of يكفهم.

mekki-muskil:58-58.t:
His saying {لنبوئنهم من الْجنَّة غرفا}: whoever reads it لنثوينهم with the thāʾ takes it from الثَّوى ("dwelling"), so غرف is accusative by omission of the preposition, because it does not take two objects. It is not good to put الغرف in the accusative as an adverb, because it is specific, and the verb does not reach a specific adverb of place except through a preposition: you do not say جلست دارا. So the implied form is "We will lodge them in chambers" (في غرف); when the preposition was omitted, it became accusative. Whoever reads it with the bāʾ makes غرفا a second object, because it takes two objects: you say بوأت زيدا منزلا ("I settled Zayd in a dwelling").
As for His saying {وَإِذ بوأنا لإِبْرَاهِيم مَكَان الْبَيْت}, the lām is redundant (zāʾida), as it is redundant in ردف لكم, which is only ردفكم; (so it means) "We settled Abraham".

mekki-muskil:66-66.t: His saying {وليتمتعوا}: whoever reads the lām with kasra makes it the lām of kay (purpose), and it may also be the lām of command. Whoever makes it vowelless, it is the lām of command and nothing else. With sukūn it cannot be the lām of kay, because after the lām of kay أن is omitted, so its vowel may not be dropped either, because of the weakness of the governors of verbs.
